M00.titleEn: Python Kickoff: Modern Tooling (uv, .venv) & How Python Runs Code
M00.summaryEn: The .py → Bytecode → CPython VM pipeline, .venv virtual environments, project management with uv, 4-space indentation & if __name__ == '__main__'

steps.headingEn: What Is Python and How Does CPython Run Your Code?
steps.bodyEn:
Welcome to your journey to master Python from scratch! This opening lesson shows you how Python executes source code under the hood and introduces the industry-standard toolchain right from day one.

Python is famous for its clean, English-like syntax, powering everything from web backends and automation to AI. Yet computers only understand binary `0`s and `1`s — so how does a machine run a `.py` file?

The reference Python runtime is called **`CPython`**. Every time you run a program, `CPython` executes a ==2-step pipeline==:

1. **Compile to `Bytecode`:** `CPython` checks the syntax of the entire `.py` file and translates it into intermediate **`Bytecode`** instructions (cached as `.pyc` files inside `__pycache__/`).
2. **Execute on the Virtual Machine (`PVM`):** The Python Virtual Machine reads each `Bytecode` instruction from top to bottom and directs the CPU to compute values, allocate memory, or produce output.

> [!NOTE] Quick Explainer
> Thanks to this `.py` → `Bytecode` → `CPython` VM mechanism, you never have to run a manual compile command beforehand: just save your `.py` file and run it immediately on macOS, Windows, or Linux!

steps.headingEn: Installing Python Locally: Traditional Setup vs Using uv
steps.bodyEn:
Before running `.py` files on your computer, you can choose **1 of 2 ways** to install Python below (**Option 2 with `uv`** is recommended because it is fast, clean, and avoids version conflicts).

### Option 1: Traditional Python Setup (`python.org` + `venv` + `pip`)

Use this when you want to install the official distribution directly from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/):

- **Windows:** Download the `.exe` installer from `python.org/downloads` → on the very first screen, **make sure to check `"Add python.exe to PATH"`** before clicking *Install Now* (if you forget, your Terminal will report that `python` is not recognized).
- **macOS:** Download the `.pkg` installer from `python.org` or install via Homebrew: `brew install python@3.12`.
- **Linux (Ubuntu / Debian):** Open Terminal and run `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip`.

Once installed, for each project you **manually create a virtual environment (`.venv`)** to isolate packages (preventing version conflicts between Project A and Project B), then install dependencies with `pip`:

```bash
python3 --version                 # Kiểm tra cài đặt thành công (Windows gõ: python --version)
mkdir my_app && cd my_app
python3 -m venv .venv             # Tạo thư mục môi trường ảo .venv thủ công

# Kích hoạt .venv trước khi cài gói hoặc chạy code:
source .venv/bin/activate         # macOS / Linux (trên Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate)
pip install requests              # Cài thư viện ngoài bằng pip
pip freeze > requirements.txt     # Xuất danh sách thư viện để chia sẻ
python app.py                     # Chạy chương trình
```

### Option 2: All-in-One Setup & Management with `uv` (Recommended)

**`uv`** (written in Rust, installing packages 10–100x faster than `pip`) unifies downloading Python, creating `.venv`, installing packages, and running code into **one single tool** — you don't even need to download installers manually from `python.org`:

```bash
# Bước 1: Cài đặt công cụ uv (chỉ làm 1 lần duy nhất trên máy)
# macOS / Linux:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
# Windows (PowerShell):
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

# Bước 2: Để uv tự tải Python 3.12 và khởi tạo dự án
uv python install 3.12            # Tự tải & quản lý Python 3.12 (không cần bộ cài python.org)
uv init my_app && cd my_app       # Sinh sẵn pyproject.toml, .python-version & main.py
uv add requests                   # Tự tạo .venv, cài gói & khóa phiên bản vào uv.lock
uv run app.py                     # Tự động dùng đúng .venv để chạy (không cần activate thủ công!)
```

| Criterion | Traditional (`python.org` + `pip`) | Modern with `uv` |
|---|---|---|
| Installing Python | Visit `python.org`, remember `Add to PATH` | Single command `uv python install 3.12` |
| Virtual env `.venv` | Manually run `python -m venv .venv` & `activate` | Auto-created and auto-used by `uv run` |
| Dependency management | Manual `pip install` + `requirements.txt` | `uv add` + `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock` |

> [!TIP] Open the Visual Setup Guide Anytime
> You can click **More → Setup Guide (`uv` / Without `uv`)** in the toolbar to compare project directory layouts, `pyproject.toml`, and step-by-step commands for each operating system.

steps.headingEn: Core Syntax Rule: 4-Space Indentation Defines Code Blocks
steps.bodyEn:
Many languages use curly braces `{ }` to mark the body of a conditional or function. Python removes curly braces completely and uses **leading indentation (4 spaces by convention)** together with a trailing colon `:` on the header line to define code blocks:

```python
age = 20

# Dòng mở khối kết thúc bằng dấu hai chấm (:)
if age >= 18:
    print("Đủ tuổi đăng ký")     # Thụt vào 4 dấu cách -> nằm TRONG khối if
    print("Chào mừng bạn!")      # Cùng mức thụt 4 dấu cách -> vẫn thuộc khối if

print("Dòng này luôn chạy")      # Sát lề trái (cột 0) -> đã ra NGOÀI khối if

# Đặt tên biến & hàm theo chuẩn snake_case (chữ thường nối bằng dấu gạch dưới)
user_full_name = "Nguyễn An"

def say_hello(name):
    return f"Xin chào, {name}!"  # f-string chèn giá trị biến trực tiếp vào { }
```

> [!WARNING] Common Pitfall
> In Python, ==indentation is a mandatory syntax rule==, not cosmetic formatting! Being off by even 1 space or mixing `Tab` and `Space` characters will immediately halt Python with an `IndentationError` before the program even starts running.

steps.headingEn: Direct Execution vs Importing as a Module: Why if __name__ == "__main__": Matters
steps.bodyEn:
A `.py` file can be used in **two ways**:
1. **Run directly** (`uv run python calculator.py`): Python automatically sets the special variable `__name__` to `"__main__"`.
2. **Imported (`import`) into another file** to reuse its functions (or loaded by an automated test grader): `__name__` holds the module's file name (`"calculator"`), not `"__main__"`.

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Chạy thử:", add(3, 5))
```

Thanks to the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard, a single file can run standalone while remaining safe to `import` without accidentally triggering test `print()` or `input()` calls.

steps.headingEn: Output with print() and the Interactive REPL Sandbox
steps.bodyEn:
The `print()` function writes values to the screen; customize the separator between arguments with `sep` and the trailing character with `end`:

```python
print("Python", 3, "dễ đọc")               # Python 3 dễ đọc (mặc định sep=" ")
print("2026", "11", "22", sep="-")         # 2026-11-22
print("Đang tải...", end=" ")              # Không xuống dòng
print("Hoàn tất!")                         # Đang tải... Hoàn tất!
```

Running `uv run python` in your Terminal opens the **REPL** (*Read – Eval – Print Loop*): type an expression after `>>>`, press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to see the result immediately (type `exit()` to quit).

> [!TIP] Easy Trick to Remember
> Open the REPL and try typing `import this` — you'll see *"The Zen of Python"*, 19 aphorisms capturing Python's philosophy of clear, explicit, and elegant code!

steps.headingEn: Learning Path from Zero & Extended Reference Comparison
steps.bodyEn:
Lesson codes (`M25`, `M26`...) are technical identifiers; simply follow the **Curriculum** order shown in the app from top to bottom (`M00` → `M25` → `M26` → `M27` → `M28` → `M01`...). Each module follows a 5-step loop: read visual theory steps → answer Quizzes → write auto-graded Exercises → read real-world code → review Flashcards.

If you have worked in the web ecosystem before, the table below maps familiar concepts to their Python equivalents:

| JavaScript / Node.js | Python | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `node app.js` | `uv run python app.py` | `uv` picks the right Python version & `.venv` automatically |
| `package.json` + `package-lock.json` | `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock` | Declares dependencies & pins exact versions |
| `node_modules/` | `.venv/` | Isolated dependency environment per project |
| `npm install axios` | `uv add httpx` / `uv add requests` | Installs packages from PyPI |
| `{ ... }` blocks & `camelCase` | `4-space` indentation & `snake_case` | Colon `:` opens a block; `#` starts a comment |
| `require.main === module` | `if __name__ == "__main__":` | Prevents script entry-point code from running on `import` |


### Deep Dive into M00's Under-the-Hood Concepts (For Beginners)
- **Where do `__pycache__/` and `.pyc` files come from?** When a Python file is imported, CPython caches the compiled Bytecode inside `__pycache__/filename.cpython-312.pyc` so future runs load almost instantaneously. You never edit these files manually, and you should always add `__pycache__/` to `.gitignore`.
- **`SyntaxError` vs `Runtime Error`:** Step 1 (compiling to Bytecode) scans the entire file before anything runs: if line 50 is missing a `:`, not even line 1 will execute. By contrast, a runtime error like dividing by `0` only triggers in Step 2 when the PVM reaches that exact line.
- **The Dunder Variable `__name__` (two underscores before and after):** Dunder (*Double Underscore*) refers to special system attributes managed by Python. When you run `uv run python app.py` directly, Python sets `__name__ = "__main__"`. When another file runs `import app`, Python executes `app.py` from top to bottom with `__name__ = "app"` — the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard keeps test/CLI entry code from firing unintentionally on import!
- **Keyword Arguments in `print("A", "B", sep="-", end="\n")`:** Named parameters passed with `=`, such as `sep="-"` (the separator between items, defaulting to a space) and `end="\n"` (the trailing character, defaulting to a newline `\n`), let you control formatting without manual string concatenation.

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- `CPython` compiles `.py` source files to `Bytecode` and executes them on the `PVM` virtual machine.
- Use `.venv` to isolate dependencies per project; `uv` manages `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, and Python versions in one tool.
- 4-space indentation after a `:` is mandatory syntax for code blocks; name variables and functions in `snake_case`.
- Always place script entry code or `input()` calls under `if __name__ == "__main__":` so the file stays safe when imported.

readings.noteEn: A small **exemplary** Python file: cleanly separated functions, a docstring, `main()`, and `if __name__ == "__main__":`.
readings.taskEn: Identify: (1) which function only performs computation vs. which performs I/O? (2) Which line corresponds to `require.main === module`?
readings.answerEn: `decide_winner()` only computes (easy to test); `get_user_choice()` uses `input()`; `main()` coordinates the flow. The final line `if __name__ == "__main__": main()`.

readings.noteEn: A flashy 'Hello world' using `time.sleep`. Not broken, but an example of top-level side effects: importing this file immediately runs it and sleeps for 7 seconds.
readings.taskEn: Refactor it so nothing executes when imported (hint: wrap it in `main()`).

M00.q1.qEn: In a modern standard Python project, which file declares the project name, Python version, and list of required dependencies?
M00.q1.explainEn: pyproject.toml is the standard PEP 621 central configuration file for a Python project, while uv.lock pins the exact versions of the entire dependency tree.

M00.q2.explainEn: When given multiple comma-separated arguments, print() automatically joins them with a single space by default (sep=' ') and ends with a newline.

M00.q3.qEn: In Python, incorrect indentation is only a cosmetic style issue and the code still runs normally.
M00.q3.explainEn: Completely false: Python uses indentation levels (4 spaces by convention) instead of curly braces to define block scope. Misaligned indentation immediately raises an IndentationError.

M00.q4.qEn: What is the purpose of placing startup code inside an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block?
choicesEn: Makes the program run twice as fast on CPython
Runs that block only when the file is executed directly, not when another file imports it
It is mandatory in every Python file or Python raises a SyntaxError
M00.q4.explainEn: When running a file directly with python file.py, __name__ equals '__main__' so the block executes; when another file imports it, __name__ holds the module name, so the entry-point block is safely skipped.

M00.q5.qEn: What is the role of the `.venv` directory in a Python project?
choicesEn: Stores an isolated virtual environment containing packages installed specifically for that project, preventing conflicts with other projects
Holds the application's primary source code to push to GitHub
Logs the history of commands typed in the Terminal
M00.q5.explainEn: .venv (Virtual Environment) isolates each project's Python interpreter and all of its packages in a separate sandbox so projects on the same machine never overwrite each other's versions.

M00.q6.explainEn: The sep='-' parameter replaces the space between 'x' and 'y' with a hyphen, and end='!\n' appends an exclamation mark at the end of the line before the newline.

M00.q7.qEn: According to Python's PEP 8 style guide, what is the standard naming convention for variables and functions?
M00.q7.explainEn: PEP 8 specifies lowercase words joined by underscores (snake_case) for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes, and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants. Note that kebab-case is parsed as subtraction in Python!

M00.c1.frontEn: Which `uv` command adds an external library (e.g., `requests`) to your project?
M00.c1.backEn: `uv add requests` — automatically updates `pyproject.toml`, locks versions in `uv.lock`, and installs the package into `.venv`.

M00.c2.frontEn: How do you run `app.py` inside the project's virtual environment using `uv`?

M00.c3.frontEn: What is the standard guard so script code only runs when executed directly (and not when imported)?

M00.c4.frontEn: How do you write a single-line comment and define a code block in Python?
M00.c4.backEn: Use `#` for comments; use `:` at the end of the header line together with **4-space indentation** for the code block.

M00.c5.frontEn: What are the main steps in `CPython`'s execution pipeline for a `.py` file?
M00.c5.backEn: `.py` source code → compiled to **`Bytecode`** (`.pyc`) → executed instruction by instruction on the **Python Virtual Machine (`PVM`)**.

greet.promptEn:
Write a function `greet(name)` that returns (using `return` — **not** `print`) a Vietnamese greeting string:

- `greet("Sơn")`  → `"Xin chào, Sơn!"`
- If `name` is empty or contains only spaces → `"Xin chào, bạn!"`
- Strip leading and trailing whitespace from `name`: `greet("  An ")` → `"Xin chào, An!"`

Syntax hint: `name.strip()` ≈ `name.trim()` in JS; f-string: `f"Xin chào, {name}!"` (keep the exact string literal `"Xin chào, ...!"` and `"bạn"` as expected by the tests).
hintsEn: First: `name = name.strip()`.
An empty string is falsy just like in JS: `if not name:` means `name == ''`.
Remember `return` — a function without `return` returns `None` (≈ `undefined`).

average3.promptEn:
Write `average3(a, b, c)` returning the arithmetic mean, **rounded to 2 decimal places** using `round(x, 2)`.

- `average3(1, 2, 3)` → `2.0`
- `average3(1, 2, 2)` → `1.67`

Unlike JS: the `/` division operator in Python **always** returns a `float`: `6 / 3 == 2.0`.
hintsEn: Compute `(a + b + c) / 3` and wrap it in `round(..., 2)`.

M25.titleEn: Terminal, File Paths & Reading Error Tracebacks
M25.summaryEn: Terminal navigation (pwd, ls, cd), absolute/relative paths, running code with uv, and reading Tracebacks from bottom to top

steps.headingEn: What Is the Terminal and How Is a Command Structured?
steps.bodyEn:
Before writing complex programs, beginners often stumble over 3 foundational skills outside Python syntax: navigating the Terminal, specifying file paths, and calmly reading error messages.

Graphical interfaces (Finder on macOS, File Explorer on Windows) let you double-click to open folders. The **Terminal** (command-line interface) does the exact same job through text commands — faster, more precise, and the standard environment for running Python, test suites, and production servers.

Every command you type in the Terminal follows a clear 3-part structure and ends with <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

```bash
tên_lệnh   --tùy_chọn   đối_số_đầu_vào
# Ví dụ:
ls -la Homework
```

Here `ls` is the action (list directory contents), `-la` is an option flag (show details including hidden dotfiles such as `.venv`), and `Homework` is the target directory. In VS Code, you can toggle the integrated Terminal with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>`</kbd>.

steps.headingEn: 8 Essential Navigation Commands on macOS / Linux
steps.bodyEn:
Mastering these 8 foundational commands covers almost every daily project workflow:

| Command | Memorable Meaning | Real Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pwd` | **Where am I?** (*Print Working Directory*) | `pwd` → `/Users/an/PyLearn` |
| `ls` | **What files/folders are here?** | `ls` or `ls -la` (shows `.venv` too) |
| `cd name` | **Step into** a subfolder | `cd Homework` |
| `cd ..` | **Go up** one level (to parent folder) | `cd ..` |
| `cd ~` | **Go home** (your personal Home folder) | `cd ~` |
| `mkdir name` | **Create** a new empty folder | `mkdir exercise_1` |
| `cat file` | **Quickly view** a text file's contents | `cat hello.py` |
| `clear` | **Clear** the Terminal screen (<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>L</kbd>) | `clear` |

> [!TIP] Easy Trick to Remember
> Never type long filenames in full! Type the first 2–3 letters and press <kbd>Tab</kbd> so the Terminal auto-completes the rest accurately; press the up arrow <kbd>↑</kbd> to recall recent commands; and press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to immediately abort a hung program.

steps.headingEn: Absolute Paths vs Relative Paths
steps.bodyEn:
To tell Python where `hello.py` lives on disk, the operating system uses two addressing styles:

- **Absolute Path:** Always starts from the filesystem root `/` (for example, `/Users/an/PyLearn/Homework/hello.py`). Like a full street address with house number, street, district, and city — no matter where you currently are, it always points to the exact same location.
- **Relative Path:** Does not start with `/`; it is resolved ==starting from the Terminal's current working directory==. `.` represents the current directory, while `..` represents the parent directory immediately above.

```text
PyLearn/
├── Homework/
│   └── hello.py
└── WorkPath/        <-- Giả sử Terminal của bạn đang đứng ở đây
```

If you are standing in `WorkPath/` and want to point to `hello.py` in the sibling folder `Homework/`, the correct relative path is `../Homework/hello.py` (step up with `..`, then enter `Homework/`).

steps.headingEn: Running Python Files and Quick Experiments with uv
steps.bodyEn:
Once you are in the project directory, `uv` commands let you launch Python consistently without worrying about system-wide version mix-ups:

```bash
uv run python                  # Mở bàn thử nghiệm tương tác REPL (thoát bằng exit())
uv run python hello.py         # Thực thi toàn bộ mã nguồn trong file hello.py
uv add rich                    # Cài vĩnh viễn thư viện rich vào dự án hiện tại
uv run --with rich python x.py # Chạy thử x.py kèm thư viện rich tạm thời không cần cài
```

steps.headingEn: Anatomy of a Traceback: Read from BOTTOM to TOP
steps.bodyEn:
When something goes wrong, Python halts execution and prints a detailed error report called a **`Traceback`**. Instead of reading from top to bottom, the fastest way is to read ==backwards from the last line up==:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/an/PyLearn/app.py", line 12, in <module>
    ket_qua = tinh_trung_binh(100, 0)
  File "/Users/an/PyLearn/app.py", line 4, in tinh_trung_binh
    return tong / so_luong
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

The 3-step `Traceback` reading workflow:
1. **Bottom line:** `ZeroDivisionError: division by zero` states the **error type** and **reason** (dividing by `0`).
2. **The `File "...", line N` line right above it:** Pinpoints the exact **filename and line number** that failed (`line 4`).
3. **The frames above:** Show the chain of function calls that led to that failing line.

steps.headingEn: Common Exceptions & Two Classic Beginner Mistakes
steps.bodyEn:
| Error Name | Quick Meaning | Common Cause |
|---|---|---|
| `SyntaxError` | Invalid syntax | Missing `:`, unclosed `)` or quote `"` |
| `IndentationError` | Misaligned indentation | Uneven 4 spaces, empty body after `:` |
| `NameError` | Undefined variable/function | Typo, missing assignment, or missing `import` |
| `TypeError` | Incompatible types | Adding string and int `"5" + 3`, calling `len(None)` |
| `ValueError` | Right type, invalid value | Casting letters to int `int("abc")` |
| `IndexError` / `KeyError` | Out-of-bounds index / missing key | Accessing `[1, 2][5]` or `{"a": 1}["b"]` |
| `FileNotFoundError` | File does not exist | Wrong working directory or misspelled filename |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` | Missing `import` library | Forgot `uv add <pkg>` or ran outside `uv run` |

> [!WARNING] Common Pitfalls
> 1. **Running a file from the wrong directory:** Running `uv run python hello.py` prints `No such file or directory` — immediately run `pwd` and `ls` to verify you are inside the folder containing `hello.py`.
> 2. **Shadowing standard library modules with filenames:** Never name an exercise file `random.py`, `math.py`, or `json.py`, because `import` will load your own file instead of Python's built-in library!


### Decoding Path & Traceback Symbols in M25
- **Spaces and command flags in Terminal:** If a folder name contains spaces (like `My Project`), wrap it in quotes: `cd "My Project"`. Short flags use one dash and can be combined (`ls -la` = `-l` + `-a`), while long flags use two dashes (`--version`).
- **Three special path symbols:** `.` (single dot) is the current directory (`./app.py`); `..` (double dot) steps up one parent directory (`../../data.csv` steps up 2 levels); `~` is your user home directory (`/Users/your_name`).
- **What `in <module>` and `~~~^~~~` mean in a Traceback:** When a Traceback says `File "app.py", line 12, in <module>`, `<module>` means the error occurred at the top level of the file (outside any `def` function). The caret markers `~~~^~~~` (Python 3.11+) underline the exact sub-expression that raised the error on that line.


| JS / Node.js Ecosystem | Python (`uv`) Equivalent | Notes for JS Developers |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `node index.js` | `uv run main.py` *(or `python3 main.py`)* | Run a single script directly |
| `npx <tool>` | `uvx <tool>` *(or `uv tool run`)* | Run a CLI tool without permanent installation |
| Stack Trace read **TOP TO BOTTOM** | `Traceback` read **BOTTOM TO TOP** | The last line of a Python Traceback holds the error name and root cause! |

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- Check your current location with `pwd`, list files with `ls`, change directories with `cd`, and step up one level with `cd ..`.
- Paths starting with `/` are absolute; paths without a leading `/` are relative to your current working directory.
- Read every `Traceback` from the bottom line up: the last line gives the error type + cause, and the last `File ..., line N` frame points directly to the line to fix.

readings.noteEn: The shortest possible Python program. Try running `uv run python printing_hello_world.py` (inside the Python-master folder) to practice: standing in the right directory and typing the exact filename.

Deliberately triggers several error types (division by zero, undefined variable, invalid eval syntax) and catches them. Read it to recognize each exception name — you'll learn exception handling in M31.

M25.q1.qEn: In the Terminal, what does the command `cd ..` do?
choicesEn: Moves up to the parent directory (one level above)
Deletes all files in the current directory
Jumps directly to the personal Home directory
M25.q1.explainEn: The double dot '..' always represents the immediate parent directory; therefore 'cd ..' moves you up one directory level. To jump straight to your Home directory, use 'cd ~'.

M25.q2.qEn: You want to know **which directory you are currently in** in the Terminal. Which command should you type?
M25.q2.explainEn: pwd stands for Print Working Directory (prints the full path of your current folder), whereas ls lists the files inside that folder.

M25.q3.qEn: When reading a multi-line Python `Traceback`, where are the **error type and immediate cause** located?
choicesEn: The first line of the Traceback
The last line of the Traceback
The first File line at the top
Python does not print error reasons
M25.q3.explainEn: A Traceback records the call stack in chronological order (most recent call last), so the actual failure point along with the exception name and detailed message always appears on the very last line.

M25.q4.qEn: When running your program, you hit `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'`. What is the standard fix in a `uv`-managed project?
choicesEn: Delete the import requests line so the code stops throwing errors
Run `uv add requests` to install the library into the project's `.venv`
Rename your current script file to `requests.py`
Uninstall Python and reinstall from scratch
M25.q4.explainEn: ModuleNotFoundError indicates a third-party package is missing from the .venv virtual environment. Running 'uv add requests' installs it into .venv and records it in pyproject.toml. Never rename your script to requests.py, as that causes circular self-import errors!

M25.q5.explainEn: print() automatically converts the integer 3 into its string representation and inserts a default space between the two arguments 'Python' and 3.

M25.q6.qEn: A `Traceback` should be read from top to bottom, ignoring the final line.
M25.q6.explainEn: Quite the opposite: the golden rule is to read a Traceback from BOTTOM TO TOP — check the last line for the error type and cause, then look at the 'File ..., line N' line immediately above it to see which line to fix.

M25.q7.qEn: Your Terminal is currently in `WorkPath`. The file `hello.py` is inside `Homework` (a sibling folder sharing the same parent directory as `WorkPath`). Which relative path is correct?
M25.q7.explainEn: Because Homework is not inside WorkPath but is a sibling folder, you must use '..' to step up from WorkPath to the shared parent directory first, then enter Homework/hello.py.

M25.q8.qEn: Evaluating `10 / 0` in Python raises which exception type?
M25.q8.explainEn: 10 / 0 is valid syntax with valid numeric types, but division by zero is mathematically undefined, so at runtime Python raises the specialized ZeroDivisionError.

M25.q9.explainEn: The string 'python' has 6 characters so len('python') returns 6; indexing in Python is 0-based, so 'python'[0] retrieves the first character 'p'.

M25.c1.frontEn: Which Terminal command tells you what directory you are currently in?

M25.c2.frontEn: What do the four commands `ls`, `cd`, `mkdir`, and `cat` each do?
M25.c2.backEn: `ls` lists files/folders · `cd` changes directory · `mkdir` creates a new folder · `cat` prints a file's contents to the screen.

M25.c3.frontEn: What do the three path symbols `.`, `..`, and `~` mean?
M25.c3.backEn: `.` is the current directory · `..` is the parent directory (one level up) · `~` is your personal Home directory.

M25.c4.frontEn: What is the standard command to run `your_file.py` using `uv`?

M25.c5.frontEn: What is the fastest order for reading a Python `Traceback`?
M25.c5.backEn: Read from **bottom to top**: last line = exception name + reason; the `File "...", line N` immediately above it = file and failing line.

M25.c6.backEn: `TypeError`: wrong data type (`"5" + 3`). `ValueError`: right type, but invalid content/value (`int("abc")`).

M25.c7.frontEn: When you get a `FileNotFoundError` running a script, what should you check first?
M25.c7.backEn: Run `pwd` and `ls` to verify whether your Terminal is in the folder containing the file and whether the filename's casing matches.

parse_traceback.promptEn:
Write `parse_traceback(text)` taking a **raw** traceback string and returning a dict:

```python
{"type": "ZeroDivisionError", "message": "division by zero", "file": "app.py", "line": 7}
```

- Extract `type` and `message` from the **last line** (`Type: reason`; split on the **first** `": "` — the reason itself may contain colons).
- Extract `file` and `line` (an integer) from the **last** `File "...", line N, ...` line (where the error actually occurred).
- If there is no `File` line → set both `file` and `line` to `None`.

Hints: `text.strip().splitlines()`, `line.strip().startswith('File "')`, `line.split('"')`, `str.partition(": ")`.

`error_type, _, message = lines[-1].partition(": ")`
Loop over each line; whenever `line.strip().startswith('File "')`, update `file` and `line_no` (the last match wins).
`stripped.split('"')[1]` gives the filename; `stripped.split("line ")[1].split(",")[0]` gives the line number — remember `int(...)`.

| `IndexError`, `KeyError`, `AttributeError` | `"truy cập"` *(access)* |
| `FileNotFoundError` | `"file"` |

split_path.titleEn: Split Path into Folder and Filename
split_path.promptEn:
Write `split_path(path)` returning the tuple `(folder, filename)`, split at the **last** `/`:

- `split_path("a/b/c.txt")` → `("a/b", "c.txt")`
- `split_path("c.txt")` → `("", "c.txt")`
- `split_path("/home/son/hello.py")` → `("/home/son", "hello.py")`

Also write `extension(path)` → file extension (including the dot) or `""` if none:

hintsEn: If `"/" in path`: `folder, _, name = path.rpartition("/")`. `rpartition` splits at the last occurrence.
When `/` is absent, `rpartition` returns `("", "", path)` — exactly what we want!
`extension`: get the filename via `split_path`, then if `"." in name`, return `"." + name.rsplit(".", 1)[1]`.

join_path.titleEn: Join Path Segments with a Single /
join_path.promptEn:

- `join_path("a/", "/b", "c.txt")` → `"a/b/c.txt"`

- `join_path("a", "", "b")` → `"a/b"` (skip empty segments)
- `join_path()` → `""`

(Python includes `pathlib`, but implement this yourself to understand paths as strings.)
hintsEn: `parts` is a tuple. Normalize each segment: the first non-empty part only needs `rstrip("/")`, while later parts need `strip("/")`.
Skip segments that are empty (after normalization), then `"/".join(...)`.

M26.titleEn: First Program: print, Variables & Your First Functions
M26.summaryEn: Input → Process → Output flow, print vs strings, variable assignment, input(), def/return functions (vs print) and f-strings

steps.headingEn: Python Program Execution Flow: Sequential Top-to-Bottom
steps.bodyEn:
Every major software system in the world — from banking apps to AI tools — ultimately boils down to 3 basic beats: receiving input data, transforming it through variables and functions, and emitting output.

A simple Python program is a plain text file ending in `.py`. When you run `uv run python thu.py`, the interpreter reads and executes **one line at a time from top to bottom**, left to right — just like following steps on an assembly instruction sheet:

```python
# Dòng bắt đầu bằng dấu # là ghi chú (Comment) dành cho con người đọc — Python bỏ qua hoàn toàn
print("Bước 1: Khởi động máy")
print("Bước 2: Pha cà phê")      # Ghi chú cũng có thể đặt ở nửa sau của dòng code
```

If line 1 hits an error, Python halts immediately at line 1 and never executes line 2.

steps.headingEn: The print() Statement: Literal Text vs Evaluated Expressions
steps.bodyEn:
The `print()` function displays information in the Terminal. The first distinction beginners must master is **quoted text** versus **unquoted expressions**:

```python
print("5 + 3")             # Có nháy -> chuỗi văn bản (str): in đúng chữ 5 + 3
print(5 + 3)               # Không nháy -> biểu thức toán học: tính trước rồi in 8
print("Tổng là:", 5 + 3)   # Ghép nhãn chữ và kết quả phép tính -> Tổng là: 8
print()                    # Gọi print() rỗng để in ra một dòng trống
```

You can wrap text strings in either single quotes `'...'` or double quotes `"..."`, as long as the closing quote matches the opening quote.

steps.headingEn: Variables: Labeling Data & Right-to-Left Assignment
steps.bodyEn:
To keep intermediate results instead of computing and losing them, we use **variables**. In school math, `=` means "the left side equals the right side." In Python programming, however, a single `=` is **assignment**, working ==from RIGHT to LEFT==: Python evaluates the expression on the right first, then binds the variable name on the left to that result!

```python
ten_khach = "Minh"
so_ly = 2
so_ly = so_ly + 1          # Bước 1: lấy so_ly cũ (2) + 1 = 3. Bước 2: gắn lại tên so_ly vào 3
print(ten_khach, so_ly)    # Minh 3
```

Mandatory variable naming rules in Python:
- Use only letters, digits, and underscores `_`; **never start with a digit** (`2gia` → `SyntaxError`, whereas `gia_2` is valid).
- Names are case-sensitive (`Tuoi` and `tuoi` are two completely different variables).
- Never use language keywords (`if`, `for`, `def`, `return`...) and **avoid shadowing built-in functions** like `list`, `str`, `sum`, or `print` or you will lose access to the original built-in for the rest of the file!

steps.headingEn: Reading User Input with input()
steps.bodyEn:
The `input("Prompt: ")` function pauses the program, waits for the user to type on the keyboard and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, and returns what they typed:

```python
ho_ten = input("Bạn tên là gì? ")
nam_sinh = int(input("Bạn sinh năm nào? "))   # Ép chuỗi sang số nguyên ngay khi nhận
tuoi = 2026 - nam_sinh
print("Xin chào", ho_ten, "- năm nay khoảng", tuoi, "tuổi")
```

> [!WARNING] Common Pitfall
> `input()` ==ALWAYS returns a string (`str`)==, even when the user types only digits like `25`! Without wrapping it in `int(...)` or `float(...)` to convert it to a number, `input() + 1` will immediately crash with `TypeError`.

steps.headingEn: Defining Functions (def) and return vs print()
steps.bodyEn:
When a piece of logic needs to be reused multiple times, we package it into a **function** using the `def` keyword: the function accepts inputs via parameters, processes them inside its body, and uses `return` to send the result back to the caller. (Think of a function like a coffee machine: parameters are the ingredients going in, and `return` is the finished drink handed out for further use.)

```python
def tinh_tien(don_gia, so_luong):   # Dòng tiêu đề kết thúc bằng dấu hai chấm (:)
    thanh_tien = don_gia * so_luong # Thân hàm bắt buộc thụt lề 4 dấu cách
    return thanh_tien               # Trả giá trị thật ra bên ngoài hàm

hoa_don_1 = tinh_tien(25000, 2)     # hoa_don_1 nhận giá trị số 50000
tong_cong = hoa_don_1 + 15000       # Tính toán tiếp dễ dàng -> 65000
```

Many beginners confuse `print()` and `return` inside a function body. Look closely at the difference:

```python
def gap_doi_sai(x):
    print(x * 2)      # Chỉ HIỂN THỊ chữ lên màn hình, không có return -> hàm trả về None!

def gap_doi_dung(x):
    return x * 2      # TRẢ VỀ con số thực sự để bên ngoài hứng lấy và dùng tiếp

a = gap_doi_dung(5) + 1   # 11 (chạy mượt mà)
b = gap_doi_sai(5) + 1    # In ra 10 rồi báo lỗi TypeError: không thể lấy None + 1!
```

> [!TIP] Easy Trick to Remember
> Every automated exercise grader and software test calls your function and inspects its **`return` value**. Whenever a prompt says *"Write a function that returns..."*, always finish with `return result` — never substitute `print(result)` for `return`!

steps.headingEn: Default Parameters, Multiple Return Values & f-strings
steps.bodyEn:
Python functions also support default parameter values when the caller omits an argument, and can return multiple values at once (packaged under the hood as a `tuple`):

```python
def chao_mung(ten, danh_xung="Bạn"):
    return f"Xin chào {danh_xung} {ten}!"   # f-string: đặt chữ f trước dấu nháy, chèn biểu thức vào { }

def hinh_chu_nhat(dai, rong):
    dien_tich = dai * rong
    chu_vi = (dai + rong) * 2
    return dien_tich, chu_vi                # Trả về 2 giá trị cùng lúc

s, p = hinh_chu_nhat(5, 3)                  # Nhận gọn vào 2 biến: s = 15, p = 16
print(chao_mung("Lan"))                     # Xin chào Bạn Lan!
print(f"Diện tích = {s}, nửa chu vi = {p // 2}")
```

**`f-string`** syntax (`f"... {expression} ..."`) is the cleanest, most readable way to combine text and values in modern Python — inside curly braces `{ }`, you can place both variable names and inline expressions.


### Deep Dive: 2-Phase Assignment, Function Calls `()`, and Tuple Unpacking
- **Why is `so_ly = so_ly + 1` valid?** `=` is not an algebraic equality check, but a **2-phase assignment**: Phase 1 evaluates the entire right-hand side (`so_ly + 1`) using the old value; Phase 2 rebinds the label `so_ly` to the new result.
- **Function definition `def` vs Function call `ten_ham()`:** Writing `def tinh_tien():` only stores the blueprint in memory (none of the body runs yet). The function only executes when called with parentheses `tinh_tien(...)`. When `return` is reached, the function exits immediately (any lines below `return` never run) and its local variables are cleaned up.
- **How `return dien_tich, chu_vi` works:** The comma `,` automatically packs the 2 values into a **`tuple` `(15, 16)`**. Outside, writing `s, p = hinh_chu_nhat(5, 3)` triggers **Tuple Unpacking** (assigning by position: the first variable gets index 0, the second gets index 1).
- **Printing literal `{` or `}` inside an `f-string`:** Because `{...}` interpolates expressions, to print literal curly braces in an `f-string`, simply double them as `{{` or `}}`.


| JavaScript / TypeScript | Python 3.12+ | Migration Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `console.log("Hi", name)` | `print("Hi", name)` | `print()` separates items with a space and ends with a newline automatically |
| `let x = 10; const PI = 3.14;` | `x = 10` and `PI = 3.14` | Python has no `let`/`const`/`var` keywords |
| `` `Hello ${name}` `` | `f"Hello {name}"` | Prefix the quote with `f` and use `{}` instead of `${}` |
| `function add(a, b = 1) { return a + b; }` | `def add(a, b=1): return a + b` | Uses `def`, `:`, and 4-space indentation instead of `{}` |

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- Quoted `"..."` is a text string; unquoted is a variable or expression; `#` starts a comment.
- `=` evaluates the right-hand side first and binds the variable on the left; `input()` always returns a `str`.
- Define functions with `def func_name(...):`, indent by 4 spaces, and use `return` to output a real value (a function without `return` returns `None`).
- Use `f"Hello {name}"` for clean string formatting without manual concatenation.

M26.q1.explainEn: The first line is inside double quotes so Python prints the literal string '5 + 3'; the second line has no quotes so Python evaluates the arithmetic expression 5 + 3 to 8 before printing.

M26.q2.explainEn: Assignment '=' always evaluates the right side first: it takes the current value of tuoi (20), adds 1 to get 21, and then rebinds the variable name tuoi to the new value 21.

M26.q3.qEn: Which variable name below violates Python's syntax rules?
M26.q3.explainEn: Python variable names may only start with a letter or an underscore (_), never with a digit, so '2gia' raises a SyntaxError.

M26.q4.explainEn: Calling nhan_doi(21) passes x = 21 into the function body, computes 21 * 2 = 42, and sends 42 back via return so print() displays it.

M26.q5.explainEn: Calling a(5) executes print(x * 2) inside the function, printing '10'. However, because function a has no return statement, it implicitly returns None into ket_qua, so the last line prints 'None'.

M26.q6.qEn: `input()` automatically returns an integer (`int`) if the user only types digits such as `25`.
M26.q6.explainEn: input() always returns a text string (str) — i.e., the string '25', not the number 25. To do arithmetic, you must explicitly cast it using int(input(...)).

M26.q7.explainEn: In an f-string (prefixed with f before the opening quote), any expression inside { } is evaluated and interpolated into the string; '2 + 3 =' outside { } remains literal text.

M26.q8.explainEn: The function doi(1, 2) returns the pair (2, 1); unpacking assignment x, y = doi(1, 2) assigns x = 2 and y = 1, so print(x, y) outputs '2 1'.

M26.q9.qEn: Why do data-processing functions and coding exercises always require `return` instead of just `print`?
choicesEn: Because print is forbidden inside Python functions
Because only a returned value can be stored in a variable, used in further calculations, and verified automatically by tests
Because return uses fewer lines of code than print
Just an arbitrary convention; the two statements are identical
M26.q9.explainEn: print() only writes text to the screen for humans to read and returns None, whereas return hands real data back out of the function so other code or automated tests can use and verify it.

M26.c1.frontEn: In `x = x + 1`, in what order does the single `=` operator execute?
M26.c1.backEn: It is **right-to-left assignment**: evaluate `x + 1` on the right first, then bind the variable `x` to the new result.

M26.c2.frontEn: What is the core difference between `print()` and `return` inside a function?
M26.c2.backEn: `print()` only displays text on screen and returns `None`. `return` exits the function and hands back a real value for reuse.

M26.c3.frontEn: What is the standard syntax to define a function in Python?
M26.c3.backEn:
```python
def func_name(params):
    return result
```
Includes `:` at the end of the `def` line and a body indented by 4 spaces.

M26.c4.frontEn: What data type does `input()` always return, and how do you convert it to an integer?
M26.c4.backEn: Always returns a string (`str`). Wrap it in `int(input("..."))` to convert to an integer.

M26.c5.frontEn: How do you embed variables and expressions directly into a string using an `f-string`?
M26.c5.backEn: Put `f` right before the opening quote and wrap expressions in `{ }`: `f"Hello {name}, sum = {a + b}"`.

M27.summaryEn: Arbitrary-precision int vs float, /, //, %, **, operator precedence, round() banking rounding, and handling 0.1 + 0.2 precision issues

steps.headingEn: Two Core Numeric Types: int (Integers) and float (Floating-Point Numbers)
steps.bodyEn:
Arithmetic in Python feels as familiar as a pocket calculator while supporting signature features like arbitrary-precision integers and the highly useful floor-division and modulo pair.

Python clearly distinguishes between two numeric types based on **whether a decimal point is present**:

```python
so_luong = 42             # int: số nguyên dương, âm hoặc 0
nhiet_do = -3.5           # float: số thực có phần thập phân
ty_le = 5.0               # Vẫn là float (dù phần lẻ bằng 0) vì có dấu chấm!
dan_so = 100_000_000      # Dấu gạch dưới _ giúp mắt dễ đọc hàng triệu, giá trị vẫn là 100000000
sieu_lon = 2 ** 200       # int trong Python tự mở rộng bộ nhớ: không bao giờ bị tràn số (Overflow)!
```

In many lower-level languages, integers are locked to 32-bit or 64-bit widths (overflowing into negative numbers beyond roughly 9 quintillion). By contrast, Python's **`int` type has arbitrary precision** — as long as your machine has RAM available, you can compute `2 ** 1000` accurately down to the very last digit!

steps.headingEn: The Seven Arithmetic Operators and the //, % Pair
steps.bodyEn:
| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result | Important Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+`, `-`, `*` | Addition, subtraction, multiplication | `7 * 2` | `14` | If either operand is a `float`, the result is a `float` |
| `/` | **True Division** | `7 / 2` ; `6 / 3` | `3.5` ; `2.0` | ==Always returns a `float`== even when dividing evenly! |
| `//` | **Floor Division** | `7 // 2` | `3` | Rounds down to the nearest integer (quotient) |
| `%` | **Modulo** (Remainder) | `7 % 2` | `1` | Remainder left over after floor division |
| `**` | **Exponentiation** (Power) | `2 ** 10` | `1024` | Careful: `^` in Python is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation! |

Imagine you have `130` seconds and want to convert them into minutes and remaining seconds:
- Whole minutes: `130 // 60` → `2` (minutes)
- Remaining seconds: `130 % 60` → `10` (seconds)
- The built-in function `divmod(130, 60)` computes both in one step, returning the tuple `(2, 10)`!

Three everyday practical uses of the `%` operator:
1. **Even / odd / divisibility checks:** `n % 2 == 0` is even; `n % k == 0` means `n` is divisible by `k`.
2. **Extracting the units digit:** `2026 % 10` → `6` (pair with `2026 // 10` → `202` to peel off digits one by one).
3. **Clock / calendar wrap-around:** `(current_hour + 5) % 24` ensures the result always wraps cleanly within `0..23`.

steps.headingEn: Operator Precedence & Augmented Assignment (+=)
steps.bodyEn:
Python follows standard mathematical precedence: **Parentheses `()` → Exponentiation `**` → Unary negation `-x` → Multiplication/Division `* / // %` → Addition/Subtraction `+ -`**. Two subtle cases frequently show up in trick questions:

```python
print(2 + 3 * 4)      # 14   (nhân trước cộng sau; muốn cộng trước hãy viết (2 + 3) * 4 -> 20)
print(-3 ** 2)        # -9   (** mạnh hơn dấu trừ đứng trước, nên hiểu là -(3 ** 2); muốn 9 viết (-3) ** 2)
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)    # 512  (riêng ** kết hợp từ PHẢI sang TRÁI: tính 3 ** 2 = 9 trước, rồi 2 ** 9 = 512)
```

To update a variable in place, use the augmented assignment operators `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `//=`:

```python
diem = 10
diem += 5             # Viết gọn của diem = diem + 5 -> 15
diem *= 2             # 30
```

> [!NOTE] Quick Explanation
> Python **does not have** `x++` or `x--` operators. To increment a counter by 1, the only standard syntax is `x += 1`.

steps.headingEn: Built-in Math Functions & round()'s Banker's Rounding
steps.bodyEn:
```python
abs(-15)              # 15     — giá trị tuyệt đối (luôn không âm)
max(4, 19, 7)         # 19     — tìm số lớn nhất (tương tự min() tìm số nhỏ nhất)
int(3.9)              # 3      — cắt bỏ thẳng phần thập phân về phía 0 (KHÔNG làm tròn!)
round(3.14159, 2)     # 3.14   — làm tròn lấy 2 chữ số sau dấu chấm
round(2.5)            # 2      — nằm đúng chính giữa .5 -> làm tròn về SỐ CHẴN gần nhất!
round(3.5)            # 4      — nằm đúng chính giữa .5 -> làm tròn về SỐ CHẴN gần nhất!
```

The *Round Half to Even* rule (rounding `.5` ties to the nearest even integer) is the international financial and statistical standard, preventing cumulative positive bias across millions of rounding operations.

steps.headingEn: Numeric Comparisons & Chained Range Conditions
steps.bodyEn:
The comparison operators `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` always evaluate to a boolean `True` or `False`. Notably, Python lets you write **chained comparisons** just like mathematical notation on paper:

```python
print(5 == 5.0)           # True — so sánh giá trị toán học nên 5 bằng 5.0
tuoi = 22
print(18 <= tuoi <= 60)   # True — kiểm tra gọn tuổi nằm trong đoạn [18, 60]
```

steps.headingEn: Why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3? Handling Precision Properly with math.isclose() and Decimal
steps.bodyEn:
If you type `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` in Python, it surprisingly evaluates to `False` because `0.1 + 0.2` produces `0.30000000000000004`! This is not a Python bug, but a fundamental property of computer hardware (the `IEEE-754` standard): just as the fraction `1/3` cannot be written finitely in base 10 (`0.33333...`), the fraction `1/10` (`0.1`) is an infinitely repeating fraction in binary (`0` and `1`), so the CPU must round it at the 53rd bit.

```python
import math
from decimal import Decimal

# Cách 1: Khi tính toán khoa học / hình học -> dùng math.isclose() thay cho ==
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))                  # True (cho phép độ lệch cực nhỏ ~1e-9)

# Cách 2: Khi tính tiền tệ / hóa đơn tài chính -> tính bằng số nguyên int (đơn vị đồng/xu) hoặc Decimal
gia_chinh_xac = Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2")      # Lưu ý: truyền CHUỖI "0.1" vào Decimal!
print(gia_chinh_xac == Decimal("0.3"))               # True tuyệt đối 100%
```

> [!WARNING] Common Mistake
> Never use `==` directly to compare two `float` values after decimal arithmetic, and when using `Decimal`, always pass a string like `Decimal("0.1")` (if you write `Decimal(0.1)` without quotes, the binary rounding error has already slipped in before `Decimal` receives it!).


### Understanding `_` Digit Separators, `1e-9`, and `int(-3.9)` vs `-3.9 // 1`
- **Underscore `_` digit separators (`100_000_000`) and `1e-9` notation:** The `_` character is purely for human readability of thousands/millions; Python ignores it completely in memory (`100_000 == 100000`, and `int("100_000")` is also valid). The notation `1e-9` is a `float` literal shorthand for $1 \times 10^{-9} = 0.000000001$.
- **Return type of `//` with a `float` operand:** `7 // 2` returns `3` (`int`), but if either operand is a `float`, such as `7.0 // 2`, the result is `3.0` (type **`float`**!). Always remember the invariant identity: `a == (a // b) * b + (a % b)`.
- **Difference on negative numbers between `int(-3.9)` and `-3.9 // 1`:** `int(-3.9)` **truncates the fractional part toward 0**, giving **`-3`**, whereas floor division `-3.9 // 1` **rounds down toward negative infinity**, giving **`-4.0`**!


| JavaScript / TypeScript | Python 3.12+ | Conversion Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `Math.floor(7 / 2)` $\rightarrow$ `3` | `7 // 2` $\rightarrow$ `3` | Built-in floor division operator `//` |
| `Math.pow(2, 10)` or `2 ** 10` | `2 ** 10` $\rightarrow$ `1024` | Python's `int` grows dynamically and never overflows like JS `Number` |
| `x++` / `x--` | `x += 1` / `x -= 1` | Python has **NO** `++` or `--` operators |
| `x >= 0 && x <= 100` | `0 <= x <= 100` | Python supports chained comparisons just like standard math |

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- `int` is exact with arbitrary precision; `/` always produces a `float`, whereas `//` gives the floor quotient and `%` gives the remainder.
- Use parentheses `()` when combining `**` with a negative sign (`-3 ** 2 == -9`); increment variables with `x += 1`.
- For `float` values, use `math.isclose(a, b)` for equality checks, and use `int` (smallest unit) or `Decimal("...")` for currency calculations.

M28.summaryEn: 5 core types, Strong Typing, explicit casting int()/float()/str(), short-circuit logic and/or/not, Truthy/Falsy, and is None

steps.headingEn: Five Foundational Data Types & Type Checking with isinstance()
steps.bodyEn:
Every value in Python has a specific data type that determines which operations are allowed on it and how Python evaluates True / False conditions.

At the most basic level, every single value in a Python program belongs to one of these 5 types:

| Python Type | Name | Examples | Primary Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int` | Integer | `0`, `42`, `-15` | Counting quantities, index positions, exact discrete math |
| `float` | Floating-point | `3.14`, `2.0`, `-0.5` | Physical measurements, percentages, continuous coordinates |
| `str` | String | `"Hello"`, `'42'`, `""` | Text, names, raw input read from keyboard or files |
| `bool` | Boolean | `True`, `False` | Logical truth values (first letters `T` and `F` MUST be **capitalized**!) |
| `NoneType` | Special null | `None` | Marking "no value yet" or a function with no `return` value |

To inspect a variable's type while debugging, use `type(x)`. When writing type-checking logic in production code, Python best practices always recommend **`isinstance(x, target_type)`**:

```python
gia = "42"
print(type(gia))                 # <class 'str'> — trông giống số nhưng thực chất là chuỗi chữ!
print(isinstance(42, int))       # True
print(isinstance(3.5, (int, float)))  # True — kiểm tra thuộc 1 trong nhiều kiểu cùng lúc
```

steps.headingEn: Strong Typing: Why Does "5" + 3 Immediately Raise an Error?
steps.bodyEn:
Python combines two very clear properties:
- **Dynamic Typing:** You don't need to declare a fixed type for a variable name; assigning `x` to the number `10` first and later reassigning it to the string `"ten"` is completely valid.
- **Strong Typing:** Python ==never performs implicit type coercion== between text and numbers! When Python sees `"5" + 3`, it doesn't know whether you want string concatenation `"53"` or numeric addition `8`, so it stops immediately and raises `TypeError` to protect you from silent calculation bugs.

```python
# "5" + 3         -> TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str!
print("5" + "3")  # "53"     — cộng hai chuỗi = nối liền đuôi nhau
print(5 + 3)      # 8        — cộng hai số = tổng đại số
print("ha" * 3)   # "hahaha" — nhân chuỗi với số nguyên n = lặp lại chuỗi n lần
```

steps.headingEn: Explicit Type Casting (int, float, str, bool)
steps.bodyEn:
To convert between types, call the target type's constructor directly:

```python
print(int("120") + 5)      # 125    — chuyển chuỗi chữ số nguyên sang int
print(float("2.75"))       # 2.75   — chuyển chuỗi thập phân sang float
print(int(3.99))           # 3      — cắt bỏ phần lẻ (KHÔNG làm tròn lên 4)
print("Điểm: " + str(10))  # "Điểm: 10" — chuyển số sang chuỗi (hoặc dùng f"Điểm: {10}")
```

> [!WARNING] Common Mistake
> Calling `int("3.5")` directly raises a **`ValueError`** because the decimal point `.` is not a valid integer digit! If your input is a decimal string and you want the integer part, convert in two steps: `int(float("3.5"))` → `3`.

steps.headingEn: Boolean Logic (not, and, or), Short-Circuit Evaluation & the in Operator
steps.bodyEn:
The three logical keywords have precedence from highest to lowest: **`not` → `and` → `or`**:
- `not a`: Inverts true to false and false to true.
- `a and b`: True only when **both** sides are true.
- `a or b`: True when **at least one** side is true.

Python evaluates `and` / `or` using **`Short-Circuit Evaluation`**: as soon as the left operand already determines the final result, Python **stops immediately and does not evaluate the right operand**! This is extremely useful for guarding against division by `0` or `None` values:

```python
so_luong = 0
tong_diem = 85

# Nhờ ngắn mạch: so_luong > 0 là False nên Python DỪNG NGAY, không chạy phép chia 85 / 0 ở vế phải!
if so_luong > 0 and (tong_diem / so_luong) >= 5.0:
    print("Đạt yêu cầu")

# Toán tử in kiểm tra một phần tử có nằm trong chuỗi / danh sách hay không:
print("py" in "python")                # True
print("Sun" in ("Sat", "Sun"))         # True
```

steps.headingEn: Truthy and Falsy Values in Conditions
steps.bodyEn:
In an `if` or `while` statement, you don't have to write an explicit `==` comparison. Every value in Python, when passed through `bool(x)`, falls into one of two categories:

- **`Falsy` group (treated as False — only these exact "empty / zero" values):**
  `False`, `None`, zero (`0`, `0.0`), the empty string `""`, and all empty collections (`[]`, `{}`, `set()`, `()`).
- **`Truthy` group (treated as True):** ==Every other value== — including the string `"0"`, the string `"False"`, and the list `[0]` (because each has length 1 and is not empty!).

```python
danh_sach_cho = []
if not danh_sach_cho:                  # Cách viết chuẩn Python thay cho if len(danh_sach_cho) == 0:
    print("Hàng đợi đang trống!")
```

steps.headingEn: The None Value & Two Subtle Pitfalls
steps.bodyEn:
`None` is the single unique object (*singleton*) representing the absence of a value. Always check for it using **`x is None`** or **`x is not None`** (never write `x == None`).

> [!TIP] Easy to Remember
> There's an interesting fact in Python's design history: `bool` is actually a subclass of `int` (`True` has numeric value `1`, `False` has `0`). Because of that, `isinstance(True, int)` returns `True`! If you write a type-classification function, always check `isinstance(x, bool)` **before** checking `isinstance(x, int)`.

| JavaScript / Node.js | Python | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `"5" + 3` → `"53"` (implicit coercion) | `"5" + 3` → `TypeError` | `Strong Typing` catches silent bugs immediately |
| `Boolean([])` and `Boolean({})` are `true` | `bool([])` and `bool({})` are `False` | Empty collections in Python are always `Falsy` |
| `null` and `undefined` | Only `None` (`x is None`) | A single, unambiguous null concept |


### Decoding the `bool("False")` Trap, Double Parentheses in `isinstance`, and `not > and > or`
- **⚠️ Classic trap: both `bool("False")` and `bool("0")` are `True`!** For `str`, **only the empty string `""` is `False`**. Any string with at least 1 character (even `"False"`, `"0"`, or a single space `" "`) passed to `bool(...)` returns **`True`**!
- **Why does `isinstance(x, (int, float))` have two pairs of parentheses?** The outer pair belongs to the `isinstance(...)` function call, while the inner `(int, float)` is a **`tuple`** grouping the allowed types ("`x` is an `int` OR a `float`").
- **Why does `"5" + 3` raise an error while `"ha" * 3` works?** The `*` operator between a `str` and an `int` is explicitly defined in Python as **string repetition** (`"ha" * 3 -> "hahaha"`, `"ha" * 0 -> ""`).
- **Logical operator precedence:** Without parentheses, Python always evaluates **`not` first ➔ `and` next ➔ `or` last** (for example, `True or False and False` evaluates `False and False` first to `False`, then `True or False` to `True`).

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- Five core types: `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `NoneType`; check types with `isinstance(x, target_type)`.
- Python will not implicitly add strings and numbers: convert explicitly with `int()`, `float()`, `str()`.
- Memorize the `Falsy` set: `False, None, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, set(), ()`; check `None` using `is None`.

M28.q7.explainEn: When int() receives a string argument, it only accepts valid integer digits; encountering the decimal point in '3.5' raises a ValueError. To convert it, call int(float('3.5')).

M28.q8.explainEn: In Python, bool is a subclass of int so isinstance(True, int) is True; None is a singleton so None is None is True, and None is not equal to 0 (False).

M28.q9.explainEn: Multiplying string 'ab' by 3 repeats it 3 times into 'ababab'; the 'in' operator checks membership of a substring in a string and an element in a list, both returning True.

M28.q10.explainEn: input() always returns a string (str) in every case; the programmer must explicitly cast it with int() or float() to perform numeric calculations.

M28.c2.frontEn: Which function inspects a type while debugging, and which function checks a type in code?
M28.c2.backEn: `type(x)` to inspect the type · `isinstance(x, int)` to safely check the type in code.

M28.c3.frontEn: Why does `int("3.5")` raise `ValueError`, and how do you handle it properly?

M28.c6.frontEn: What is the PEP 8 standard syntax to check if variable `x` is `None`?

M28.c7.frontEn: Why must you check `isinstance(x, bool)` before `isinstance(x, int)` when classifying types?
M28.c7.backEn: Because `bool` inherits from `int` in Python (`isinstance(True, int)` is `True`), so checking `int` first would catch `bool` values.

M01.summaryEn: Object-reference model on the Heap (id, is vs ==), floor division on negatives, value-returning logic operators, tuple swap & pure functions

steps.headingEn: How Python Manages Memory: Variables Are Reference Labels Pointing to Objects
steps.bodyEn:
After getting comfortable with basic operations and types, this lesson takes you inside Python's memory model to understand the true nature of variables, object references, and the subtlest operator rules.

In languages like C or Java, a variable is often thought of as a fixed memory slot bound to a data type. In Python, however, memory management follows **`Pass-by-Object-Reference`**: every piece of data (`100`, `"Son"`, `[1, 2]`) is an **Object allocated on the Heap**, carrying its own type and a unique address identifier visible via `id(obj)`. A **variable name is simply a reference label pointing to that object** in memory (like a sticky tag attached to an item):

```python
x = 100              # Tạo đối tượng int(100) trên Heap, gắn tên x trỏ tới nó
y = x                # Tạo thêm tham chiếu y trỏ tới CÙNG đối tượng int(100) đó (không sao chép dữ liệu!)
x = x + 1            # Số int bất biến -> tạo đối tượng int(101) MỚI và dời x sang 101; y vẫn trỏ 100!

gio_a = [1, 2]       # Danh sách list là đối tượng KHẢ BIẾN (Mutable — sửa được nội dung bên trong)
gio_b = gio_a        # Cả gio_a và gio_b cùng trỏ vào ĐÚNG MỘT danh sách trên Heap
gio_b.append(99)     # Sửa bên trong đối tượng qua gio_b...
print(gio_a)         # [1, 2, 99] -> nhìn qua gio_a cũng thấy bị thay đổi theo!
```

Understanding that ==variables are reference labels pointing to objects== is essential for explaining the behavior of `list`, `dict`, and function parameters in upcoming lessons.

### Memory Model Deep Dive: Why on a `list`, `b = b + [99]` Leaves `a` Unchanged While `b += [99]` Mutates `a` Too?

When `a = [1, 2]` and `b = a` (both pointing to the same memory address `0x100`):
- **Writing `b = b + [99]`**: The `+` operator always **allocates a BRAND-NEW `list` object (`0x200`)** containing `[1, 2, 99]`, then detaches label `b` from `0x100` and points it to `0x200`. Thus `a` still points to `0x100` (`[1, 2]`), completely unaffected!
- **Writing `b += [99]`**: On a mutable `list`, the `+=` operator invokes the in-place method (`__iadd__`, equivalent to `b.extend([99])`) — it **appends `99` directly into the existing `0x100` object** without creating a new one! As a result, both `a` and `b` see `[1, 2, 99]`.

steps.headingEn: Clearly Distinguishing == (Value Equality) and is (Object Identity)
steps.bodyEn:
Because two different variable names can point to two separate objects with identical contents, or share the exact same object, Python provides two distinct operators:

- **`a == b` (Value equality):** Checks whether the **internal contents** of the two objects are equal. Use this for almost all comparisons of numbers, strings, and lists.
- **`a is b` (Identity comparison):** Checks `id(a) == id(b)` — whether the two labels point to the **exact same physical object in memory**. Use this only for special singletons like `x is None`, `x is not None`.

```python
ds_1 = [10, 20]
ds_2 = [10, 20]              # Tạo một danh sách thứ hai độc lập có cùng các con số
print(ds_1 == ds_2)          # True  — nội dung hai danh sách giống hệt nhau
print(ds_1 is ds_2)          # False — nhưng là hai đối tượng nằm ở hai địa chỉ nhớ khác nhau!
```

> [!WARNING] Common Beginner Trap
> Never use `is` to compare numbers or text strings (such as `if x is 1000:` or `if name is "admin":`)! CPython internally caches small integers `-5..256`, which can trick you into thinking `is` works during quick tests, only to fail unpredictably on larger numbers. Always use `==` for values and reserve `is` for `None`!

steps.headingEn: Floor Division (//) and Modulo (%) on Negative Numbers
steps.bodyEn:
Earlier we saw `7 // 2 == 3`. But what happens with `-7 // 2`? The name of `//` is *Floor Division* (rounding down toward negative infinity on the number line), not truncation toward `0`:

```python
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2)     # 3.5 và 3
print(-7 / 2, -7 // 2)   # -3.5 nằm giữa -4 và -3 -> làm tròn XUỐNG sàn nhỏ hơn là -4!
print(-7 % 3)            # 2! Vì Python luôn giữ đẳng thức: (-7 // 3) * 3 + (-7 % 3) = (-3)*3 + 2 = -7
```

Having `%` take the sign of a positive divisor (`-7 % 3 == 2`, always staying in `0..2`) is an elegant mathematical design: when stepping backward around a clock or a circular array `(index - 1) % size`, the result is always a valid non-negative index!

steps.headingEn: and / or Return the Deciding Operand & Chained Comparisons
steps.bodyEn:
In fact, `a or b` and `a and b` do not simply coerce the result to `True`/`False`; they **return the actual operand that determined the outcome** via `Short-Circuit Evaluation`:

```python
# or dừng và trả về toán hạng Truthy ĐẦU TIÊN (nếu tất cả Falsy thì trả về toán hạng cuối):
ten_nhap = ""
ten_hien_thi = ten_nhap or "Khách ẩn danh"    # "" là Falsy -> trả về "Khách ẩn danh"

# So sánh chuỗi kép tự nhiên (điểm số vừa >= 0 vừa <= 100):
diem = 85
hop_le = 0 <= diem <= 100                     # True (tương đương diem >= 0 and diem <= 100, nhưng chỉ tính diem 1 lần)
```

steps.headingEn: Simultaneous Assignment, Swapping a, b = b, a & Constant Conventions
steps.bodyEn:
Thanks to `Tuple Packing and Unpacking`, you can assign multiple variables on a single line or swap two variables without needing a temporary `temp` variable:

```python
rong, cao = 1920, 1080
rong, cao = cao, rong        # Xoay dọc màn hình: vế phải gói (1080, 1920) trước rồi gán lại cho rong, cao!
MAX_RETRIES = 3              # Python không có từ khóa khóa cứng hằng số; viết IN_HOA để báo hiệu không sửa đổi
```

steps.headingEn: Clean Function Design: Separating Pure Computation from input() / print()
steps.bodyEn:
In many beginners' scripts, `input()`, interest formulas, and `print()` are all mixed together at the top level of the file. That style of code cannot be imported elsewhere or tested automatically.

> [!TIP] Easy to Remember
> Always separate your program into 2 distinct layers: **Pure computation functions** (taking `int`/`float`/`str` parameters and returning clean results via `return`) and an **I/O entry block** placed under `if __name__ == "__main__":`.

| JavaScript / Node.js | Python | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `===` (strict equality) | `==` (value) & `is` (same object) | Python doesn't implicitly coerce types on `==`, so no `===` is needed |
| `Math.trunc(-7 / 2)` → `-3` | `-7 // 2` → `-4` (`int(-7 / 2)` → `-3`) | `//` floors down the number line; `%` keeps the divisor's sign |
| `-7 % 3` → `-1` | `-7 % 3` → `2` | Very convenient for positive circular array indexing |
| `const MAX = 3` | `MAX = 3` (`UPPER_CASE` convention) | Signals a constant to readers and type checkers |


### Decoding Reference Counting (Garbage Collection) & the `0 or default` Trap
- **Where does the old object in RAM go when a variable is reassigned?** Every object on the Heap keeps a count of how many labels point to it (*Reference Count*). When you assign `x = 100` and later reassign `x = 200`, the reference count on `int(100)` drops to `0`, and Python's *Garbage Collector* automatically reclaims that memory.
- **Operand-return rules for `and` vs `or` and the `0` trap:**
  - `A or B` stops at the first `Truthy` value: returns `A` if `A` is `Truthy`, otherwise returns `B`.
  - `A and B` stops at the first `Falsy` value: returns `A` if `A` is `Falsy`, otherwise returns `B`.
  - **⚠️ Real-world trap:** If you write `score = input_score or 10` to fall back to a default when a score is missing, and a student actually scores **`0` (`input_score = 0`)**, since `0` is `Falsy`, `0 or 10` turns a `0` into `10`! When `0` or `""` is a valid value and you only want to replace `None`, write explicitly: `input_score if input_score is not None else 10`.
- **Do not chain-assign mutable objects (`a = b = []`):** Writing `a = b = []` makes both `a` and `b` point to the exact same single empty list on the Heap! Initialize them on separate lines: `a = []` and `b = []`.

steps.headingEn: Key Takeaways
steps.bodyEn:
- Variables in Python are reference labels pointing to objects on the Heap (`id()`); assigning `b = a` shares the same object rather than copying it.
- Use `==` to compare value equality; only use `is` / `is not` when checking identity with `None`.
- `//` floors down the number line (`-7 // 2 == -4`), `%` preserves the divisor's sign (`-7 % 3 == 2`), and `a, b = b, a` swaps two variables in one step.

M01.q1.explainEn: '/' always returns a float (3.5); '//' is floor division (rounds down to the greatest integer less than or equal to the exact quotient), so 3.5 becomes 3 while -3.5 floors down to -4.

M01.q2.qEn: What does the expression `"1" + 1` produce in Python?
M01.q2.explainEn: Python is strongly typed, so it does not implicitly coerce between str and int. You must write explicitly '1' + str(1) or int('1') + 1.

M01.q3.qEn: In Python, an empty list `[]` evaluated in `if []:` is treated as True (`Truthy`).
M01.q3.explainEn: In Python, all empty collections ([], {}, set(), ()) as well as the empty string '', 0, and None are Falsy. This lets you cleanly check for an empty list with 'if not items:'.

M01.q4.explainEn: round() uses round-half-to-even when the fractional part is exactly .5 (2.5 -> 2, 3.5 -> 4), while int(3.9) truncates toward 0 to give 3.

M01.q5.explainEn: The chained comparison 1 < x < 10 checks both 1 < 5 and 5 < 10 simultaneously (True), while == compares numeric value so 5 == 5.0 is True.

M01.q6.qEn: What is the most PEP 8 compliant way to check whether variable `x` holds `None`?
M01.q6.explainEn: Because None is a unique singleton object in memory, PEP 8 specifies always checking identity with 'x is None' or 'x is not None'.

M01.q7.explainEn: The 'or' operator evaluates left to right and returns the first Truthy operand it encounters. Since the empty string '' is Falsy, the expression returns 'Anonymous'.

M01.q8.explainEn: In Python, the modulo result % always carries the sign of the divisor (3 > 0), so -7 = (-3)*3 + 2 gives remainder 2. Exponentiation ** is right-associative: 3 ** 2 = 9 is computed first, then 2 ** 9 = 512.

M01.c1.frontEn: What is the difference between `==` and `is` in Python?
M01.c1.backEn: `==` compares the **value/contents** inside two objects; `is` checks whether two variable names point to the **exact same object in memory** (used for `x is None`).

M01.c2.backEn: Because `//` is *Floor Division* — it always rounds **down to the smaller integer** on the number line (`-3.5` floors down to `-4`). To truncate toward `0`, use `int(-7 / 2)`.

M01.c3.frontEn: How does Python's variable model work when you assign `b = a`?
M01.c3.backEn: Variables are **reference labels** pointing to objects on the Heap. `b = a` attaches label `b` to the same object as `a` (without making a copy).

M01.c4.frontEn: What does the expression `user_input or "Default"` return?
M01.c4.backEn: It returns `user_input` itself if it is `Truthy` (non-empty); otherwise it returns `"Default"`.

M01.c5.frontEn: What is the Pythonic way to check that `score` is between `0` and `10` and that list `items` is empty?
M01.c5.backEn: Range check: `0 <= score <= 10` · Empty list: `if not items:`.

M01.c6.frontEn: How do you swap two variables `a` and `b` in one line without a temporary variable?
M01.c6.backEn: `a, b = b, a` (using `tuple` packing and unpacking).

M02.summaryEn: Unicode strings, advanced f-string formatting, bidirectional positive/negative indexing, Slicing [start:stop:step], immutability & join/split

steps.headingEn: Creating Unicode Strings: Single Quotes, Double Quotes, Multiline & Raw Strings
steps.bodyEn:
Text appears everywhere from usernames to web content; Python equips the `str` type with remarkably elegant slicing and formatting syntax.

In Python, a string (`str`) is a sequence of Unicode characters (natively supporting accented characters as well as emoji). You have 4 ways to write strings depending on the situation:

```python
loi_chao = 'Xin chào'                   # Nháy đơn và nháy kép có giá trị giống hệt nhau
trich_dan = "Cô ấy nói: 'Học Python rất vui!'"  # Bọc nháy kép bên ngoài để dùng nháy đơn bên trong
tho_nhieu_dong = """Dòng thứ nhất
Dòng thứ hai"""                         # Ba dấu nháy liên tiếp giữ nguyên các dấu xuống dòng
duong_dan = r"C:\new_folder\test.txt"   # Raw string (chữ r đầu): giữ nguyên dấu \ thay vì hiểu \n là xuống dòng!
```

steps.headingEn: Professional Formatting with f-strings
steps.bodyEn:
Beyond simple value interpolation, **`f-string`** supports a mini formatting language placed right after a colon `:` inside `{ }` — extremely useful when printing invoices, tables, or debugging:

```python
mon, gia, ma_so = "Cà phê sữa", 29500.5, 7
print(f"{mon} có giá {gia:,.0f}đ")      # 'Cà phê sữa có giá 29,500đ' (dấu phẩy tách hàng nghìn)
print(f"Tỷ lệ: {gia:.2f}")              # 'Tỷ lệ: 29500.50' (cố định 2 chữ số thập phân)
print(f"Mã vé: {ma_so:03d}")            # 'Mã vé: 007' (đệm số 0 cho đủ 3 chữ số)
print(f"|{mon:>14}|")                   # '|    Cà phê sữa|' (căn phải 14 ô; < căn trái, ^ căn giữa)
print(f"{mon=}, {ma_so * 2=}")          # "mon='Cà phê sữa', ma_so * 2=14" -> mẹo in tên biến khi debug!
```

steps.headingEn: Bidirectional String Indexing: Left-to-Right (0) and Right-to-Left (-1)
steps.bodyEn:
The string `s = "Python"` consists of 6 characters stored contiguously in memory. Python simultaneously supports ==two indexing systems== to access individual characters:
- **Positive indices (left to right):** starting from **`0`** up to `len(s) - 1` (`'P'` at `0`, `'y'` at `1`, ..., `'n'` at `5`).
- **Negative indices (right to left):** starting from **`-1`** at the last character and counting back to `-len(s)` (`'n'` at `-1`, `'o'` at `-2`, ..., `'P'` at `-6`).

```python
s = "Python"
print(len(s), s[0], s[-1], s[-2])       # 6 P n o (lấy ký tự cuối bằng s[-1] siêu gọn!)
```

steps.headingEn: Extracting Substrings with Slicing s[start:stop:step]
steps.bodyEn:
**`Slicing`** extracts a substring using the half-open interval rule **`[start : stop)`**: taking from position `start` up to **just before `stop`** (excluding index `stop`), advancing by `step` characters each time:

```python
s = "Python"
print(s[1:5])        # 'ytho'   — lấy chỉ số 1, 2, 3, 4 (độ dài luôn bằng 5 - 1 = 4 ký tự!)
print(s[:2], s[2:])  # 'Py' và 'thon' — bỏ trống đầu = từ 0; bỏ trống cuối = tới hết chuỗi
print(s[::2])        # 'Pto'    — nhảy bước 2 (lấy các vị trí 0, 2, 4)
print(s[2:999])      # 'thon'   — Slicing tự giới hạn an toàn khi vượt biên, không báo IndexError!
```

> [!TIP] Easy Rule of Thumb
> Accessing a single out-of-bounds index (`s[999]`) raises an `IndexError`, whereas `Slicing` (`s[:10]`) is always safe even on strings shorter than 10 characters — very handy for writing title truncation helpers!

### The "Dividers Between Cells" Model — How to Never Mess Up `s[start:stop]` Slicing

Why does `s = "PYTHON"` with `s[1:4]` return indices `1, 2, 3` (`"YTH"`) and stop right before `4`? Picture slice indices as sitting on the **divider lines between character cells**, like tick marks on a ruler:

```text
Vạch kẻ dương:  0     1     2     3     4     5     6
                +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
Ký tự trong ô:  |  P  |  Y  |  T  |  H  |  O  |  N  |
                +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
Vạch kẻ âm:    -6    -5    -4    -3    -2    -1
```

- When you write `s[1:4]`, you place the first blade at **tick `1`** and the second blade at **tick `4`** ➔ What lies between the two blades is the 3 cells `| Y | T | H |` (length is always `stop - start = 4 - 1 = 3`).
- **Key difference between Slicing and Indexing:** Accessing a single out-of-range cell (`s[99]`) immediately throws `IndexError`, whereas **out-of-bounds slicing (`s[1:99]`) is automatically clamped by Python to the final tick (`6`) safely without ever raising an error!**

steps.headingEn: Immutability, Reversing Strings with s[::-1] & Fast Joining with "".join()
steps.bodyEn:
In Python, `str` sits on the **Immutable** side of **`Mutable vs Immutable`**: once a string is created in memory, nobody can modify individual characters inside it!

```python
s = "hello"
# s[0] = "H"              -> TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment!
s_moi = "H" + s[1:]       # ĐÚNG: ghép tạo một đối tượng chuỗi MỚI 'Hello'
dao_nguoc = s[::-1]       # 'olleh' — bước nhảy -1 quét ngược từ cuối về đầu tạo chuỗi đảo mới
```

> [!WARNING] Common Beginner Traps
> 1. **Forgetting to capture the return value:** Because strings are immutable, calling `ten.strip()` or `ten.upper()` by itself **does not modify `ten` at all**! You must reassign it: `ten = ten.strip()`.
> 2. **String concatenation `+=` inside a large loop:** Joining thousands of text fragments in a loop with `ket_qua += manh` repeatedly reallocates memory. The Pythonic way that achieves linear ==`O(n)`== speed is collecting the fragments in a list and calling **`"".join(danh_sach)`**!

steps.headingEn: Essential Text Methods & Comparison Table
steps.bodyEn:
```python
cau = "  Xin chào Python 3  "
print(cau.strip())                      # 'Xin chào Python 3' (cắt khoảng trắng thừa ở 2 đầu)
print(cau.lower(), cau.upper())         # đổi chữ thường / chữ HOA
print("a,b,c".split(","))               # ['a', 'b', 'c'] — tách theo dấu phẩy
print("  một   hai \n ba ".split())     # ['một', 'hai', 'ba'] — split() rỗng tự gom mọi khoảng trắng!
print("-".join(["2026", "11", "22"]))   # '2026-11-22' — chuỗi phân cách gọi .join(danh_sach)
print("banana".replace("a", "o"))       # 'bonono' — thay TẤT CẢ các vị trí khớp
print("py" in "python", "123".isdigit())  # True True — kiểm tra chuỗi con & kiểm tra toàn chữ số
```

| JavaScript / Node.js | Python | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `s.length` / `s.trim()` | `len(s)` / `s.strip()` | Also has `lstrip()` (left) and `rstrip()` (right) |
| `s.includes("x")` / `s.indexOf("x")` | `"x" in s` / `s.find("x")` | `s.find` returns `-1` if missing; `s.index` raises `ValueError` |
| `arr.join("-")` | `"-".join(arr)` | The separator string acts as the receiver calling `.join()` |
| `s.replace("a", "o")` (first only) | `s.replace("a", "o")` (all) | To limit replacements: `s.replace("a", "o", 1)` |
| `s.slice(1, 4)` | `s[1:4]` (and reverse `s[::-1]`) | `Slicing` syntax is built into all sequence types |


### Decoding `f-string` Format Specifiers After `:`, Negative-Step Slicing & the `.strip()` Trap
- **Reading any specifier after `:` in `f"{gia_tri : spec}"`:**
  - `f"{gia:,.2f}"`: `,` is the thousands separator (`1,250,000`); `.2` keeps exactly 2 digits after the decimal point; `f` means *fixed-point float*.
  - `f"{ma:03d}"`: Leading `0` is the padding character; `3` is the minimum total width of 3 characters; `d` is *decimal int* ➔ `7` becomes `"007"`.
  - `f"{ten:>14}"` / `:<14` / `:^14`: Right (`>`), left (`<`), or center (`^`) alignment within a 14-character field.
  - `f"{ti_le:.1%}"`: Automatically multiplies by 100 and appends `%` ➔ `0.156` becomes `"15.6%"`.
- **Slicing with a negative step (`step < 0`):** When `step` is negative (moving right to left), `start` **must be to the right of (greater than) `stop`**! For example, to slice backwards from index 4 down to just before index 1, write `s[4:1:-1]` (writing `s[1:4:-1]` returns an empty string `""`).
- **⚠️ Trap: `s.strip("...")` vs `s.removeprefix()` / `s.removesuffix()`:** Calling `.strip(".py")` does **not** remove the suffix `".py"` as a unit — it strips every individual character in the set `{".", "p", "y"}` from both ends (turning `"puppy.py".rstrip(".py")` into `"pu"`!). To remove an exact prefix or suffix substring (Python 3.9+), always use **`s.removeprefix("...")`** and **`s.removesuffix(".py")`**!
- **Difference between `s.split()` and `s.split(" ")`:** `s.split()` (with no arguments) automatically collapses consecutive whitespace and strips leading/trailing whitespace (`" a   b ".split() -> ["a", "b"]`), whereas `s.split(" ")` splits strictly on every single space character.

steps.headingEn: Core Summary
steps.bodyEn:
